pll1d1c2-ieieas.summary: Applies Augustine's threefold division of things: those to be enjoyed make us blessed, those to be used help us toward beatitude, and we (and the holy angels) stand between as those who enjoy and use.
claims: Things to be enjoyed make us blessed.
Things to be used support us on the way to beatitude.
Humans and angels are things that enjoy and use.

pll1d1c2-faeand.summary: Defines the key terms: to enjoy is to cling in love to something for its own sake; to use is to refer what comes into use toward obtaining what is to be enjoyed; illicit use is abuse.
claims: Enjoyment is loving adherence to a thing for its own sake.
Use refers a thing to what is to be enjoyed.
Illicit use is abuse rather than use.

pll1d1c2-riqhud.summary: Identifies the objects of enjoyment as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, a single supreme thing common to all who enjoy it, while noting with Augustine the inadequacy of the word 'thing' or even 'cause' for such excellence.
claims: The things to be enjoyed are the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
The Trinity is one supreme thing, the one God.
No name adequately fits the divine excellence.

pll1d1c2-raqiec.summary: States briefly that the things to be used are the world and what is created in it.
claims: The world and creatures are things to be used.

pll1d1c2-uaitac.summary: Supports the use of the world with Augustine and Romans 1:20: the world is to be used, not enjoyed, so that through visible things the invisible and eternal are grasped.
claims: The world is to be used, not enjoyed.
Through created things the invisible things of God are known.

pll1d1c2-iieipp.summary: Adds Augustine's criterion: only eternal and unchangeable things are to be enjoyed; all else is to be used for attaining their full enjoyment.
claims: Only eternal and unchangeable things are to be enjoyed.

pll1d1c2-uaiqfe.summary: Cites De Trinitate X for a cognitive formulation: we enjoy known things in which the will rests delighted for their own sake, and use those we refer to something else.
claims: Enjoyment is the will's delighted rest in a known thing for its own sake.
Use is referring a known thing to another end.

pl-l1d1c2.summary: Introduces Augustine's division of things into those to be enjoyed (frui), those to be used (uti), and those that enjoy and use (humans and angels). Defines enjoyment as clinging in love to something for its own sake and use as referring something to the attainment of what is to be enjoyed. Identifies the Trinity as the sole object of enjoyment and the world as the object of use.
claims: Things are divided into those to be enjoyed, those to be used, and those that enjoy and use.
To enjoy is to cling in love to a thing for its own sake; to use is to refer it to obtaining what is to be enjoyed.
Only the eternal and unchangeable Trinity is to be enjoyed.
The world and created things are to be used, so that the invisible things of God may be known through them.
